About

Alexandria Bates writes songs for people who held it together when it counted, and are tired of pretending it didn't cost them anything.

She grew up in the boondocks of Onondaga County, upstate New York, in lake country where winters are long and people say what they mean. Most of her adult life has been split between garage floors and lines of code. That mix of grease and logic shows up in her music: raw on the surface, carefully built underneath.

Her music sits between alternative rock and blues-soul, built on low, gritty vocals and electric guitar that knows when to stay quiet. The songs swing between defiance and exposure. One track is a woman walking out with her head up; the next is the same woman alone late at night, letting her guard down for someone she didn't plan on. There are songs about starting over, about wanting something again after years of shutting it off, and about surviving things no one showed up for.

Very little is spelled out. The lyrics say one thing on the surface and carry something heavier underneath, which leaves room for listeners to bring their own story to it.

It's music for people whose lives didn't follow the script: the ones who never quite fit in, who built something on their own, and who are still figuring out what comes next.

She started writing in her spare time to work through her own life. Those songs became a reminder that what people think they're facing alone is more common than they know.

In her own words

I never started this with the intention of publishing anything. It was a creative outlet, a way to unload things I couldn't bring myself to talk about. Putting my experiences into a song instead of a journal entry felt like a more powerful way to vent, without emotionally taxing anyone else. Singing into the void just helped lift the weight.

I only showed a few people, and the feedback was the opposite of what I expected. They kept nudging me to share it. When I finally did, it lifted even more weight off my shoulders, and I'm still not sure why.

I don't have any expectations. If even one person finds it and enjoys it, I'll be shocked, flattered, with a side order of disbelief. I started this during a dark time, and I'm at the age where I thought I'd have more of a legacy to leave behind. Maybe this is it. So I might as well make it meaningful and worth someone's time. If years from now it means something to someone, that would be enough for me.

Alexandria Bates
